title: Cleft sentences
goal: Student emphasises any element of a clause by splitting it into two parts — the highlighted piece and the connector clause.
connects_to: M04 (Subjunctive) — moves from emphasis to mood.
module_chunks: The place where / The time when...

units.title: It was X who
units.grammar_focus: It-clefts for emphasis on subject, object, time, or place
units.real_life_context: You highlight one specific element by reframing the whole sentence around it.

grammar.sentence: _____ broke the window, not me.
grammar.explanation: It-cleft structure: "It + was/is + emphasised element + who/that + rest of clause". Here we emphasise the agent (John) by splitting "John broke the window" into "It was John who broke the window". The "who/that" follows the highlighted person.

grammar.sentence: _____ in 2015 that we first met.
grammar.explanation: Time emphasis: "It was + time + that + clause". The original "We first met in 2015" gets rebuilt around the year. Use "that" (not "when") in this cleft pattern — "when" would also work in some registers, but "that" is the cleft standard.

grammar.sentence: _____ Mary _____ called me last night, not Jane.
grammar.explanation: Subject emphasis with contrast. "It was Mary who" splits the original "Mary called me last night" so we can attach the contrast ("not Jane"). Cleft is ideal for correcting mistaken assumptions.

grammar.sentence: It was the manager which decided to cancel the project.
grammar.answer: It was the manager who decided to cancel the project.
grammar.explanation: After "It was + person", use "who" (or "that"), never "which". "Which" is for things. Common slip when speakers default to "which" as universal connector.

grammar.passage: The trial hinged on a single fact. 'It was not the defendant who pulled the trigger,' the lawyer insisted. 'It was the older brother. Until the jury accepts that, the case will keep collapsing.' Three witnesses had said the same thing in earlier testimony.
grammar.question: Who does the lawyer say actually pulled the trigger?
grammar.explanation: "It was not the defendant who pulled the trigger. It was the older brother." Cleft used twice for high-stakes emphasis — first to deny one agent, then to assert the real one.

listening_speaking.text: It was John who broke the window.
It was in 2015 that we first met.
It's the silence that gets to me.
It wasn't me who called — it was Tom.
It was at the airport that I finally cried.

units.title: What I need is
units.grammar_focus: Wh-clefts (pseudo-clefts) — What + clause + is/was + emphasised element
units.real_life_context: You hold the listener's attention by setting up an expectation ("what I need is...") then landing the key word.

grammar.sentence: _____ a good night's sleep.
grammar.explanation: Wh-cleft pattern: "What + subject + verb + is/was + emphasised element". The original "I need a good night's sleep" gets reframed to spotlight the need. Common in fluent C1 speech.

grammar.sentence: _____ how patient she stayed throughout the chaos.
grammar.explanation: "What + clause" sets up an expectation; "was + element" delivers it. Here the element is a noun clause ("how patient she stayed..."), which works fine after a wh-cleft.

grammar.sentence: _____ I did _____ apologise immediately.
grammar.explanation: "What I did was apologise immediately." Note: after "what I did was", you can use base form (no "to") — a quirk of this cleft pattern. "What I did was apologise" / "What I did was call him" — base form.

grammar.sentence: What I need is to rest, sleep, eat.
grammar.hint: After "What I need is", you can use bare nouns or a single thing
grammar.answer: What I need is rest, sleep, and food. (or: What I need is to rest, sleep, and eat.)
grammar.explanation: Original mixed an infinitive ("to rest") with bare nouns ("sleep, eat"). Either commit to nouns (rest, sleep, food) or to infinitives (to rest, to sleep, to eat). Parallelism is mandatory.

grammar.passage: The candidate dodged the policy question and went personal. 'What this country needs is leadership that listens,' he said. 'What we don't need is another decade of slogans dressed up as plans.' The audience cheered the rhythm more than the substance.
grammar.question: What does the candidate claim the country needs?
grammar.explanation: "What this country needs is leadership that listens." Wh-cleft used rhetorically. Followed by the inverse wh-cleft ("What we don't need is...") — a rhythm device common in political speech.

listening_speaking.text: What I need is a long weekend.
What surprised me was her honesty.
What he did was apologise sincerely.
What matters most is how we treat people.
What this team needs is more autonomy.

units.title: All I want is
units.grammar_focus: All-clefts and exclusive emphasis ("All I want is...", "All she did was...")
units.real_life_context: You minimise or single out — saying that one thing alone matters, or that only one act occurred.

grammar.sentence: _____ a quiet evening at home.
grammar.explanation: "All + subject + verb + is + element" = the only thing wanted is X. "All I want is" minimises the request — emphasises modesty or focus. Equivalent to "the only thing I want is...".

grammar.sentence: _____ smile politely and walk away.
grammar.explanation: "All + subject + did + was + base form". Note bare infinitive after "was" — no "to". Emphasises that her response was minimal or restrained.

grammar.sentence: _____ asked _____ a fair chance.
grammar.explanation: "All he asked for was a fair chance." The cleft holds the modesty of the request — one thing, nothing more.

grammar.sentence: All I want is to be respect.
grammar.hint: After "All I want is", use a noun or "to + base" form
grammar.answer: All I want is to be respected. (or: All I want is respect.)
grammar.explanation: "To be respect" is ungrammatical — either "to be respected" (passive infinitive) or just "respect" (noun). The all-cleft requires a clean nominal or full infinitive.

grammar.passage: When the journalist pressed him on whether he wanted revenge, he shook his head. 'All I want is the truth on the record,' he said. 'All they did was lie for fifteen years. I don't need a courtroom — I need an honest sentence in print.'
grammar.question: What does the speaker want?
grammar.answer: the truth on the record (or "an honest sentence in print")
grammar.explanation: Two all-clefts: "All I want is..." (modest demand) and "All they did was lie" (minimised act, here ironically — fifteen years of lies framed as 'all they did'). The structure can carry humility or sarcasm.

listening_speaking.text: All I want is a quiet weekend.
All she did was smile.
All he asked for was a chance.
All we need is more time.
All they did was complain.

units.title: It wasn't until
units.grammar_focus: "It + negative + cleft" — "It wasn't until... that..." for delayed realisation/event
units.real_life_context: You spotlight the late moment when something finally happened or was understood.

grammar.sentence: _____ I left home _____ I understood my parents.
grammar.explanation: "It wasn't until + clause + that + main clause" — the it-cleft form of delayed realisation. Compare to the inversion "Not until I left home did I understand..." (M02). Same idea, different structure.

grammar.sentence: _____ the second draft _____ the story started working.
grammar.explanation: Time-clause + it-cleft. "The story started working" was delayed until the second draft — the cleft drama tises the delay.

grammar.sentence: _____ I _____ the photo _____ I recognised her.
grammar.explanation: "It wasn't until I saw the photo that I recognised her." Past simple in both clauses — the delay between seeing and recognising is the point.

grammar.sentence: It wasn't until I read the contract when I noticed the clause.
grammar.hint: After "It wasn't until + clause", use "that", not "when"
grammar.answer: It wasn't until I read the contract that I noticed the clause.
grammar.explanation: "When" feels natural but breaks the cleft pattern. The cleft structure is strictly "It wasn't until X that Y". "When" works for plain temporal links, not for the cleft emphasis form.

grammar.passage: Doctors often miss the rarer diagnoses. It wasn't until the third specialist that anyone considered the autoimmune angle. By then, three years had passed and several treatments had failed. 'It wasn't until I trusted my own instincts,' the patient said, 'that I started getting answers.'
grammar.question: What finally led to answers?
grammar.answer: trusting her own instincts (or "the third specialist considering autoimmune angle")
grammar.explanation: Two it-not-until clefts: "It wasn't until the third specialist that..." and "It wasn't until I trusted my own instincts that...". Both highlight delayed turning points.

listening_speaking.text: It wasn't until I left that I understood.
It wasn't until last year that we connected again.
It wasn't until then that the penny dropped.
It wasn't until I read it twice that I caught the irony.
It wasn't until the surgery that the diagnosis became clear.

units.title: The reason is, The thing that
units.grammar_focus: Lexical clefts ("The reason (why)... is...", "The thing that... is...", "The place where...", "The time when...")
units.real_life_context: You frame an explanation, the salient feature, or the location/time precisely.

grammar.sentence: _____ I'm leaving is that I want a new challenge.
grammar.explanation: "The reason (why) + clause + is + that-clause/element". "Why" is optional in modern English ("the reason I'm leaving is..."). "Because" is incorrect here — the explanation comes after "is".

grammar.sentence: _____ surprised me _____ his lack of preparation.
grammar.explanation: "The thing that + clause + was + element". Synonymous with "What surprised me was..." (wh-cleft) but using a noun ("the thing") as anchor. Slightly more colloquial.

grammar.sentence: _____ I work _____ in a converted warehouse.
grammar.explanation: "The place where + clause + is + element". Locative cleft. Modern usage permits "The place I work is...", but "where" makes the structure explicit.

grammar.sentence: The reason why I'm tired is because I didn't sleep.
grammar.hint: After "The reason ... is", use "that" or just a clause — not "because"
grammar.answer: The reason why I'm tired is that I didn't sleep. (or: The reason I'm tired is that I didn't sleep.)
grammar.explanation: "The reason... is because" is redundant — "reason" already implies cause, and "because" duplicates it. Use "that" or simply a clause.

grammar.passage: The retiring CEO summed it up. 'The reason we succeeded was discipline, not genius. The thing that holds most companies back is the temptation to chase fashion. The time when we changed course wasn't a board meeting — it was a kitchen table conversation with my partner.'
grammar.question: According to the CEO, what causes most companies to fail?
grammar.answer: chasing fashion (or "the temptation to chase fashion")
grammar.explanation: Three layered lexical clefts: "The reason... was discipline", "The thing that holds... is the temptation to chase fashion", "The time when we changed course wasn't... it was...". Layered for rhetorical weight.

listening_speaking.text: The reason I'm leaving is that I want a change.
The thing that surprises me is how calm she is.
The place where we met is now a parking lot.
The time when I felt most alive was that summer in Spain.
The reason it works is consistency, not talent.

cross_unit_consolidation: Build it-clefts to emphasise subjects, objects, times, places ("It was X who/that...")
Use wh-clefts (pseudo-clefts) to set up and deliver emphasis ("What I need is...")
Apply all-clefts to minimise or single out ("All I want is...", "All she did was + base")
Construct "It wasn't until X that Y" for delayed realisation
Open lexical clefts with "The reason", "The thing that", "The place where", "The time when"
Choose between cleft families based on what's being emphasised
